title: The Anatomy of an Input Field
intro: Every input field has up to **7 elements**. Most teams get at least 2 wrong. The required indicator debate alone has tripped up entire design systems.

learn.title: The 7 elements of an input field
learn.text:
Every input field can have up to 7 elements. Here's the stack, top to bottom:

**1. Asterisk (*)** — Required indicator. Place it left of the label, in a standout color like red.

**2. Label** — Always visible, always present. Never rely on placeholder text as a label.

**3. Optional indicator** — Use only when mixing required and optional fields. Place right of label, in parentheses.

**4. Explanatory text** — Context-specific help. Keep it visible — don't hide it behind an "i" icon or tooltip.

**5. Input field control** — The standard input box. Users recognize it without help (40+ years of convention).

**6. Placeholder text** — Almost never use it. The article's rule: avoid it.

**7. System help text** — Goes at the bottom. For field requirements, data warnings, and status messages.

right.label: Don't
items: Put error messages above the field

try.q: Where should explanatory text (help text) be placed?
options: Visible below the label, never hidden behind a tooltip
Inside the input as placeholder
In a tooltip on an 'i' icon
Above the form as a general instruction
try.explain: Help text should be visible without interaction. Hiding it behind icons or tooltips means most users will never see it.

learn.title: Why placeholder text is almost always wrong
learn.text:
The article's position: **avoid placeholder text**. Three reasons:

**1. Filled fields look pre-filled.** When placeholder text disappears on focus, users may think a value was already entered — leading to skipped fields and errors.

**2. Accessibility problems.** Many browsers and assistive technologies don't reliably read placeholder text. It creates barriers for screen reader users.

**3. Low visual contrast.** Placeholder text is typically gray and sometimes italic — weak and easy to miss, especially for users with visual impairments.

**What to use instead:**
→ A visible label (always)
→ Explanatory text below the label for formatting hints
→ Auto-formatting to guide input (e.g., phone numbers grouping into segments)

**Also: never use floating labels.** NN/g confirms placing the label and hint outside the field is the best approach. Floating labels create usability and accessibility problems.

try.q: What does the article recommend instead of placeholder text for format hints?
options: Auto-formatting (like grouping phone number digits)
A tooltip on hover
A placeholder with higher contrast
An info icon next to the field
try.explain: Auto-formatting guides users naturally — e.g., a phone field that groups digits shows the expected format without placeholder text.

learn.title: The required indicator debate
learn.text:
The article's position: **mark every required field with an asterisk**, even when ALL fields are required.

**The counterargument:** "Just put a note at the top saying 'all fields required' — asterisks on every field add visual clutter."

**Why the article rejects that:**

→ Users focus on the field under their cursor and process one task at a time. A note at the top of the form is easily missed.
→ Users must hold that top note in working memory while filling each field. That's a cognitive burden.
→ It's a **Type 1 vs. Type 2 error** trade-off. An unmarked required field risks false negatives — users skip it, submit, hit an error. The article judges that outcome worse than visual clutter.

Bottom line: the cost of a user missing a required field is higher than the cost of visual noise from asterisks.

try.q: Why does the article say a 'top of form' note about required fields is insufficient?
options: Users focus field-by-field and easily miss top-level instructions
It doesn't meet WCAG requirements
It's slower to implement
Screen readers can't detect it
try.explain: Users process forms one field at a time. A note at the top requires them to remember it while filling every subsequent field.

test.q: How many elements can an input field have, according to the article?
options: Up to 7
Exactly 3
Up to 5
Up to 10
test.explain: The anatomy includes: asterisk, label, optional indicator, explanatory text, input control, placeholder text, and system help text.

test.q: What is the article's position on placeholder text?
options: Avoid it — it disappears, looks pre-filled, and has accessibility issues
Use it for all fields to save space
Use it only for email and password fields
Use it as a replacement for labels on mobile
test.explain: Placeholder text disappears on focus, can look pre-filled, has low contrast, and screen readers may skip it.

test.q: Why does the article recommend against floating labels?
options: They create usability and accessibility problems — NN/g says labels belong outside the field
They're too expensive to implement
They only work on iOS, not Android
They slow down form submission
test.explain: NN/g confirms that placing labels and hints outside the field is the best approach. Floating labels introduce interaction and accessibility issues.

test.q: When should you use the optional indicator (the word 'Optional' next to a label)?
options: Only when mixing required and optional fields in the same form
On every optional field in every form
Never — just use asterisks for required fields
Only on long forms with more than 10 fields
test.explain: The optional indicator is useful only when the form has a mix of required and optional fields — it helps distinguish between them.

test.q: The article frames the required-indicator debate as what kind of trade-off?
options: Type 1 vs. Type 2 error — visual clutter vs. users skipping required fields
Speed vs. accuracy in form completion
Desktop vs. mobile design patterns
Accessibility vs. aesthetics
test.explain: Asterisks add visual noise (Type 1) but unmarked fields risk users skipping them and getting submission errors (Type 2). The article says Type 2 is worse.
